weeks.title: Find what matches
weeks.objective: Match objects by one stated attribute.

connection.before: Notice familiar objects and communicate a choice.
connection.after: Keep one attribute fixed when making groups.

days: Explore pairs of familiar objects and describe what is alike.
Model matching by colour with the first example.
Try shape and size matches with sheet A.
Use sheet B to explain why a tempting object does not match the rule.
Choose a sheet C game and observe whether the child keeps the chosen rule.
explanation: This is a playful NEL preschool bridge; K is an editorial label, not a Singapore Primary 1 year or a US age equivalence. Read all activities aloud. Show two objects, name one feature such as colour, and invite the child to touch the matching object. A match depends on the named feature, not on every feature being identical.

Use large paper pieces or familiar toys that can be moved. Place a red circle beside a red square and say that these match in colour although their shapes differ. Then change the question to shape and compare the red circle with a blue circle. Let the child demonstrate before asking for words.

If the child selects a favourite object, restate the rule without calling the choice careless. Ask which visible feature the two objects share. Accept pointing and home-language explanations. Observe matching during play; these activity sheets are adult prompts, not a formal written arithmetic requirement.

weeks.objective: Sort a supplied collection consistently by one attribute.

connection.before: Match a pair by a named feature.

days: Name the feature on each of two baskets.
Model separating a mixed collection by colour.
Try sheet A with paper pieces.

explanation: Sorting puts every object in a group using the same rule. Prepare two mats, then model picking up one object, checking its colour and placing it on the appropriate mat. Keep the rule visible with a sample object so memory or reading does not become the task.

Use a small mixed collection with two clear attribute values. A red large card and a red small card belong together when colour is the rule. Move one piece at a time and check the whole collection at the end; unplaced objects are part of the problem too.

An attractive arrangement is not necessarily a consistent sort. If shapes and colours become mixed rules, ask what every object on this mat has in common. A child may suggest a different useful rule; acknowledge it, then carry out the originally agreed rule before changing it.

weeks.title: Same objects, new rule
weeks.objective: Re-sort the same collection and explain what changes.

connection.before: Apply one rule to every object.
connection.after: Infer a sorting rule from examples.

days: Sort a small set by colour.
Move the same pieces into shape groups.
Compare which partners stayed together and which moved.
Use sheet B to name two valid rules.
Let the child lead a re-sorting game from sheet C.
explanation: Keep all the pieces on the table when a rule changes. Begin with four cards: two colours across two shapes. Sorting by colour and then by shape shows that an object can belong with different companions without changing itself. Say the new rule before any pieces move.

Ask the child to describe what makes each new group a group. A blue square can leave a blue circle and join a red square when the feature becomes shape. The first sort was not wrong; the purpose has changed. Point to the sample on each mat to support attention.

Do not require overlapping groups or a two-feature grid. This week changes one rule at a time. If the child keeps the old groups, compare a deliberately contrasting pair and ask which feature now matters. Accept a demonstrated regrouping as an explanation.

weeks.title: Mystery sorting trays
weeks.objective: Infer, test and communicate a simple sorting rule.

connection.before: Re-sort a fixed set in different valid ways.

days: Model a tray with positive and contrasting examples.

explanation: A mystery tray shows a rule through examples. Give at least two members and a contrasting non-member. A tray with red circle and red triangle beside a blue circle suggests colour, because shape varies among the members while red stays the same. Ask what both members share.

Test the proposed rule with a new item before declaring it useful. If the child proposes a different rule that fits every supplied example, acknowledge that several rules can sometimes work. Add a contrasting piece or state the intended feature rather than claiming to know an unspoken intention.

The aim is clear communication and consistency. Invite the child to invent a tray and describe its rule by words or by pointing to a feature. Adults can deliberately make one placement error, then let the child repair it with evidence from the objects.

connection.before: Count collections and recognise their totals.

explanation: Place one cup opposite each toy guest. Pairing makes comparison visible without requiring numeral symbols. When every guest has one cup and every cup has one guest, the collections have the same number. Show that each pair uses one object from each collection.

connection.before: Pair collections one to one.

days: Name both sides of one comparison: more cups and fewer spoons.

explanation: More and fewer describe a relationship between two collections. If six ducks are paired with four ponds, two ducks remain unmatched. There are more ducks than ponds and fewer ponds than ducks. Say both statements while pointing to the relevant sets.

Keep quantities within ten and supply all objects or marks. Start by pairing, then count to attach number names to what the child can see. Equal is a third possibility: neither set has more when all one-to-one matches are complete.

connection.before: Describe more, fewer and equal from pairs.

days: Spread the smaller of two collections into the longer row.
Model matching to test the misleading appearance.

explanation: A long row can contain fewer objects than a short row. Establish totals or make pairs before comparing quantities. Draw connecting lines or physically move partners together so the evidence remains visible when spacing is misleading.

explanation: To compare lengths directly, straighten two strips and line up one end of each at the same mark. The strip that reaches farther is longer. A strip shifted forward can look longer even when it is shorter, so the shared starting place is part of the method.

connection.before: Align starting ends for fair length comparisons.

days: Build towers on a common tabletop.

explanation: Height is compared from a common base. Set towers on the same table and keep them upright; the top that reaches farther up belongs to the taller tower. Identical blocks make the comparison easy to reproduce, but the child can point to the result without naming measurements.

Order three objects by a stated feature: height, length or overall size for similar shapes. explanation: A repeating pattern has a chunk that occurs again in the same order. Model clap, stamp, clap, stamp and pause after a complete pair. Name the chunk “clap-stamp” and perform it again. Each action can be a gesture, sound or seated movement chosen for the child.

Lay paper pieces in a row and place a loop around each complete chunk. For red-blue-red-blue, the short repeating chunk is red-blue. The next item depends on where the row stopped: after red comes blue, and after blue a new red-blue chunk begins.

Children sometimes continue with any attractive item or simply copy the last object. Ask them to say or point through a whole chunk before extending. All tasks supply the repeating rule or enough repeats to make the intended rule clear; this is following a stated pattern, not guessing a unique law from a few terms.

explanation: A repeating chunk can contain the same member twice. Say clap-tap-tap with a small pause after the second tap, then repeat the whole chunk. The two taps belong inside one unit; a clap does not have to follow every tap. Moving a finger along three places can help.

explanation: A rectangle has four straight sides and four square corners, like the corner of a sheet of paper. Opposite sides match in length. days: Rotate a set of basic paper shapes.

explanation: A shape name describes features of an outline, not where the card is facing. Turn a triangle, square or rectangle slowly while the child keeps a finger on one side. The same sides and corners remain. Small and large copies can share a shape name too.

Make collections with deliberately varied examples: thin and wide triangles, squares resting on corners, and long rectangles turned upright. Include clear non-examples, such as an open outline or a curved-sided three-tip shape, so children check defining features rather than a familiar silhouette.

Distinguish turning from changing the boundary. Cutting a corner off a square creates an extra side; stretching a circle into an oval changes its roundness. Let children trace the before and after outlines and say what stayed or changed. Adult explanations can be informal but must refer to the actual boundary.

examples.prompt: Adult rotates a square card by a quarter turn. Explain why it is still a square.

examples.prompt: A triangle card is enlarged while keeping the same outline proportions. Is the larger copy a triangle?

explanation: Place a triangle above a square to make a house picture. The picture is one design made from two component pieces. Trace each piece and name it before tracing the whole outside edge. The outer outline does not automatically have the same name as either part.

For joining shapes into a larger rectangle or square, align complete matching edges with no gap and no overlap. Adult-prepared identical squares can sit side by side to form a non-square rectangle. Physical turning and trying are the main methods; no area formula or fraction notation is required.

Ask both “How many pieces?” and “What shapes are the pieces?” A rectangle made from two squares is one outer shape but still uses two pieces. If pieces overlap, the hidden part still exists as material but the visible picture changes. State whether the task asks about pieces or visible outlines.

explanation: The same paper pieces can make different pictures. Two triangles can be the sails of a boat or the ears of an animal; their use changes while their triangle features remain. Count and name the available pieces before building so the fixed collection stays visible.

Compare component count with whole-picture count. Four square tiles may make one large square or one long rectangle, but either arrangement still uses four square tiles. Moving pieces does not create new pieces. Trace the outside only when the question asks about the combined outline.

explanation: Count a collection of up to five objects, then move some onto each of two mats inside one tray. Each mat shows a part; the tray’s entire collection is the whole. Sweep around both mats when asking how many altogether, so the whole is not confused with the larger part.

Use spoken number bonds before equations. Say “two here and three there make five altogether” while pointing to the two groups, then bring them together and count to check. A drawing of two small loops inside one large loop can record the same relationship without requiring a written sum.

Parts need not be equal. One mat may hold all the objects while the other is empty. Zero describes that empty part. Keep every object in exactly one part: double-counting a shared object or leaving one outside breaks the partition of the original whole.

explanation: Before hiding counters, count the whole with the child and agree that none will be added or removed. Cover a part with an opaque cup while leaving the rest visible. The question concerns the hidden part, not the whole under and outside the cup together.

Build a second matching collection to reason without seeing the hidden counters. If seven were present and four remain visible, set out seven spare counters and mark four as the visible part. The three unmarked counters model the covered part. Reveal the cup to check the prediction.

connection.before: Find a hidden part from a known unchanged whole.

days: Build an eight-, nine- or ten-object whole.

Use sheet A for concrete quantity bonds.

explanation: Extend the same concrete part–whole reasoning to ten. Start with a counted whole, then use two mats, boxes or loops for its parts. A whole of ten can be shown with five objects in each row initially, but children may use any organisation that supports counting each object once.

Some stories give both parts and ask for the whole; others give the whole and one part. Listen for which quantity is unknown before moving counters. For a missing part, model the whole and separate the known part; for a missing whole, combine the two supplied parts and count.

Keep stories within the supplied objects and avoid a written algorithm. Joining and separating actions prepare later arithmetic, but the bridge observes how the child represents the situation. Ask the child to check by rebuilding the whole, and accept correct alternative partitions in open tasks.

explanation: Positional words connect one object to another. Place a toy in a box, then on the closed lid, then under the box raised on supports. Say the reference object each time. “Under” alone is incomplete if several possible objects are present.

explanation: Near and far compare distance from a named place or object. Put one toy close to a basket and another farther away, then ask which is nearer to the basket. If the reference changes to a door at the other end, the answer can change. Name the reference every time.

Behind does not always mean invisible. A taller object behind a shorter one may still be seen. Let children move and inspect scenes while keeping the agreed reference clear. If a description lacks a viewpoint or face direction, ask for that information rather than marking one possible interpretation wrong.

examples.prompt: A toy dog faces a bowl. A ball lies beyond the dog’s tail. Describe the bowl and ball relative to the dog’s own facing direction.

weeks.title: Left and right together
weeks.objective: Follow left/right and up/down directions from a fixed shared viewpoint.

days: Adult and child sit side by side facing the same page.

explanation: Left and right need an agreed viewpoint. For these paper activities, adult and child sit side by side facing the page with its top star upright. Page-left and page-right stay fixed as printed; up means toward the top star and down away from it. Adults may point and name directions first.

Use a three-place row or a small grid with a counter at a stated start. Moving one place left means entering the neighbouring place on page-left, not rotating the counter. Keep each movement separate and say where the counter lands before adding a second direction.

A person’s own left and right change their relationship to the room when the person turns. Someone facing the child can appear reversed, so do not use a facing adult’s hand as an unlabelled model. explanation: A route is an ordered set of moves. Use a small grid or path prepared from the given labels. Adult and child face the same upright page; left, right, up and down refer to that page. A move enters one neighbouring space unless another distance is explicitly stated.

explanation: A sequence places events in a useful order. In a pretend snack routine, wash hands before handling food, put food on a plate, then eat. Adults act or draw the supplied steps while reading them; the child arranges pictures or gestures rather than reading event cards independently.

Before and after depend on the named event. In “choose a book, open it, look inside”, opening is after choosing and before looking inside. Use a row of cards to point to these relationships. First and last locate ends of this particular sequence, not universal times of day.

Some orders are necessary while others are choices. A seed goes into soil before it can sprout in a simple growing story, but placing two separate empty cups on a tray can occur in either order. Accept alternative sequences when all stated dependencies are satisfied and ask the child to explain.

Count four left and include both parts for the whole.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: A sign border repeats leaf-flower. It ends leaf-flower-leaf-flower-leaf. Add the next member and name the chunk.
steps: The final leaf starts a new pair.
Flower completes that pair.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Adult presents a small rotated triangle, a large circle and a square. Which has exactly three straight sides?
steps: Trace each boundary’s features.
The triangle’s rotation and size do not change its three sides.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Adult says twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen. Continue the oral count to twenty.
steps: Continue one number word at a time after sixteen.
Stop at twenty; this task rehearses words, not a twenty-object count.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

worksheets.title: Try and explain: Run and explain our market
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each activity aloud and prepare the stated objects, drawings or actions. The child may point, move objects, speak or use a home language; no reading is assumed. Offer a few activities during short play sessions, not all sheets at once. Record the child’s strategy; drawing or numeral formation is optional unless the activity invites it.

items.prompt: A puppet labels seven goods with numeral 3 because the 3 is printed larger. How should the sign be chosen?
steps: Print size does not change a numeral’s name.
Seven one-to-one counting actions establish the quantity.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Two baskets each hold five toys, but one is spread over a bigger area. A puppet says that basket has more. Check its claim.
steps: Pair the five toys from each basket.
No unmatched toy remains in either group.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: A toy dog faces the stall. Its parcel sits on the tail side. Is the parcel in front of or behind the dog’s own facing direction?
steps: The dog’s nose identifies front.
The tail side is the opposite, back side.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Rule: clap-tap-tap. A performance is clap-tap-tap-clap-tap-wave. Repair the performance using the same rule.
items.answer: Change the last wave to tap.
steps: The first triple states the required chunk.
The final position of the second triple must match its last tap.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: An order asks for four apples. A child selects four but then counts one apple again and reports five. What should be trusted and checked?
items.answer: The physical four-apple collection, checked by moving each once.
steps: An extra touch does not create an apple.
Recount with separate counted and uncounted areas to obtain four.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: A route on a row gate-stall-pond begins at gate. A child moves right then right and says stall. Correct the destination.
steps: The first right move reaches stall.
The second right move reaches pond.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Plan a stall with exactly eight goods in two nonempty baskets and make matching quantity records. Give one valid arrangement.
items.answer: Example: 3 goods and 5 goods, with 3 and 5 marks or numeral labels.
steps: Count eight as the fixed whole.
Use every item once across the two baskets; other nonempty partitions are accepted.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Make a market decoration with a three-position repeating chunk using three different shapes. Show two copies.
steps: Choose and state the ordered three-shape chunk.
Repeat every position consistently; other three-distinct-shape orders work.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Create a three-step packing routine that puts five counted goods in a bag and closes it only afterward.
items.answer: Count out five goods, put them in the open bag, close the bag.
steps: Counting establishes the requested quantity.
Packing must precede the final closing; equivalent sensible wording works.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Build a pretend cart picture using one rectangle and two circles, then turn the whole picture. Name the unchanged components.
steps: Turning does not alter each piece’s boundary.
Count the same three components after the turn.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Choose a way to prove that an order of seven is satisfied by two groups of three and four goods.
items.answer: Combine and count 7, or match all goods to seven target spaces.
steps: Include both disjoint groups once.
A complete seven-object match supports the order; either concrete check works.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.

items.prompt: Tell or show one strategy you used successfully in the market and demonstrate it with a supplied small collection of six counters.
items.answer: Example: move each counter once into a row while saying one through six, then say six altogether.
steps: The demonstration must actually use the six supplied counters.
Accept another correct demonstrated strategy, such as splitting them three and three and reconstructing the whole.
items.skill: Select and explain concrete counting, comparison, pattern and shape strategies in an integrated play setting.
